idiom_name: module keyword as namespace: nested modules per domain area, private constants for internals
implementation_notes: Ruby's module is both a namespace and a mixin container; for this pattern it is used as the namespace - module Billing; class Invoice; end; end - with nesting mirroring the domain (Billing::Invoice). Visibility is set per method with private or protected (which affect instance methods) and per constant with private_constant, while module methods can be made private with private_class_method; there is no package-private level, and since classes and modules are open the boundary is a convention rather than an enforced rule. A gem, or a top-level module inside a host application's source tree, is the physical unit of distribution and the strongest boundary available.
code_sketch:
# billing/invoice.rb
module Billing
  class Invoice; end            # published: Billing::Invoice

  class Ledger                   # internal by convention
    private_constant :Ledger
  end
end

# clients: Billing::Invoice.new
pitfalls: Constant lookup is lexical first and then walks the ancestors chain, so a bare Invoice inside Billing can silently resolve to a top-level constant instead of Billing::Invoice - qualify references or control Module.nesting deliberately.
Modules are open: any code can reopen Billing and add or redefine methods, so encapsulation can be broken without touching the module's files.
private_class_method and private_constant must be declared explicitly and Ruby's private is bypassable with send, so internals are advisory.

Autoloading (for example Zeitwerk in Rails) maps constants to paths, so an inconsistent namespace and folder layout produces intermittent uninitialized-constant errors instead of a compile-time failure.
